The endings -mų, -mąt’ę and -xi on the verbs mean ‘saw’, ‘hit’ and ‘waited for’, respectively. The material before the verb ending identifies the object and its number; for example, pihų refers to one cedar, whų to multiple cedars, and pit’oy to multiple people.

Nouns used as subjects have endings such as -na, -ne and -nemą, with the choice depending on the noun and its number. Possessive prefixes distinguish ‘our’, ‘your’, ‘their’ and ‘his’; their form also depends on the noun and its number. For example, ąmci is ‘his eye’, whereas ąwci is ‘his eyes’.

Applying these patterns gives the following translations into English:
(a) Their people saw the cedars.
(b) His deer hit the mother.
(c) His cedars hit the people.
(d) The sparrow waited for the deers.

The translations into Taos are:
(a) kąmp’įwne ipikaxi
(b) p’ine ikimų
(c) kiwcine iwp’imų
(d) ipęna ip’ǫyxi"}

The noun stems include t’oy ‘person’, hų ‘cedar’, pę ‘deer’, ka ‘mother’, p’įw ‘sparrow’, p’ǫy ‘brother’, ci ‘eye’, p’i ‘head’ and ki ‘blanket’. The endings -mų, -mąt’ę and -xi on the verbs mean ‘saw’, ‘hit’ and ‘waited for’, respectively. The material before the verb ending identifies the object and its number; for example, pihų refers to one cedar, whų to multiple cedars, and pit’oy to multiple people.

Nouns used as subjects have endings such as -na, -ne and -nemą, with the choice depending on the noun and its number. Possessive prefixes distinguish ‘our’, ‘your’, ‘their’ and ‘his’; their form also depends on the noun and its number. For example, ąmci is ‘his eye’, whereas ąwci is ‘his eyes’.

Applying these patterns gives the following translations into English:
(a) Their people saw the cedars.
(b) His deer hit the mother.
(c) His cedars hit the people.
(d) The sparrow waited for the deers.

The translations into Taos are:
(a) kąmp’įwne ipikaxi
(b) p’ine ikimų
(c) kiwcine iwp’imų
(d) ipęna ip’ǫyxi
